qs.q: A 10-day-old preterm infant with necrotising enterocolitis shows no clinical improvement despite maximal medical therapy, and serial blood gases demonstrate a rising base deficit and increasing lactate. What category of surgical indication has this infant met?
o: A contraindication due to high risk of short bowel syndrome
A relative indication requiring prompt surgical evaluation
A minor finding managed purely by continuing medical therapy
An absolute indication demanding emergency laparotomy
qs.e: Clinical deterioration despite maximal medical therapy and a rising lactate or base deficit are classified as relative surgical indications. Pneumoperitoneum is the only absolute indication.

ai.title: Interpretation of Arterial Blood Gases
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: Arterial blood gases (ABG) reveal oxygenation, ventilation and acid‑base status, guiding urgent decisions on respiratory support and underlying pathology, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: ABG is a bedside test measuring pH, PaO2, PaCO2, HCO3‑, and SaO2 from an arterial sample, allowing assessment of oxygen delivery, ventilation and metabolic balance.
Respiratory failure is staged by PaO2 and PaCO2. Type I (hypoxemic) PaO2 < 60 mmHg with normal/low PaCO2. Type II (hypercapnic) PaCO2 > 45 mmHg with pH < 7.35.
b: Moderate: PaO2 40‑60 mmHg or PaCO2 45‑55 mmHg
Severe: PaO2 < 40 mmHg or PaCO2 > 55 mmHg

sections.p: In low‑resource surgical patients, common precipitants are:
Patients may show dyspnoea, tachypnoea, altered mental status, cyanosis, or a rapid shallow breathing pattern. Look for accessory muscle use and altered chest expansion.

t.b: What is the patient’s oxygenation, ventilation and acid‑base status? – Determines type of respiratory failure and need for ventilatory support.
What is the peripheral oxygen saturation? – Guides immediate oxygen therapy when ABG unavailable.
What structural lung problem is present? – Identifies pneumonia, pneumothorax, effusion.
What is the trend of CO2 during ventilation? – Helps monitor ventilation when ABG cannot be repeated frequently.

sections.p: Uncorrected severe hypoxemia or hypercapnia rapidly leads to cardiac arrest, cerebral edema, or multi‑organ failure.
Treat the underlying cause, then correct oxygenation and ventilation. Use simple, low‑technology methods first.
b: Give supplemental O2 to keep SpO2 > 92 % (or 88‑92 % in CO2 retainers).
If PaCO2 > 45 mmHg with acidosis, start controlled‑flow mask (88‑92 % FiO2) and monitor ABG.
Non‑invasive ventilation (BiPAP) if available and patient is cooperative.
Intubation and mechanical ventilation for severe type II failure or deteriorating consciousness.
Treat cause: antibiotics for pneumonia/TB, anticoagulation for PE, bronchodilators for asthma/COPD, chest tube for pneumothorax.

sections.p: Repeat ABG after any therapeutic change. Prevent recurrence with early mobilization, incentive spirometry, smoking cessation, and vaccination.
b: Post‑op: encourage deep breathing and ambulation.
Chronic lung disease: optimise inhaler technique, avoid sedatives.

sections.p: ABG results can be mistaken for simple pulse oximetry values or venous blood gas values.
b: Venous gas: lower PaO2, higher PaCO2; not interchangeable for ventilation decisions.
SpO2: reflects saturation only, not PaCO2 or pH.
Chronic CO2 retainers may have normal PaO2 but high PaCO2; aim for 88‑92 % FiO2.
Severe anemia lowers oxygen content despite normal PaO2.
High altitude shifts normal PaO2 lower; adjust expectations.

faq.q: Why is PaCO2 more important than SpO2 in a COPD patient?
faq.a: COPD patients retain CO2; a rising PaCO2 signals ventilatory failure even if SpO2 looks acceptable.

faq.q: Can I rely on a venous gas in an emergency?
faq.a: Venous gas gives trends but cannot replace arterial values for ventilation decisions.

faq.q: What does a high anion‑gap metabolic acidosis with normal PaCO2 mean?
faq.a: It indicates a primary metabolic problem; the lungs have not yet compensated, so watch for rapid respiratory compensation.

exam: A post‑op patient on day 2 develops tachypnoea and confusion – what ABG values would make you start non‑invasive ventilation and why — Look for PaCO2 > 45 mmHg with pH < 7.35 indicating type II failure.

You have a patient with severe asthma exacerbation, SpO2 94 % on 6 L O2, but ABG shows PaCO2 55 mmHg, pH 7.28 — what does this tell you and what is the next step — Rising CO2 signals impending respiratory arrest; intubate promptly.

In a rural hospital without ABG, a patient with suspected pulmonary embolism is hypoxic — how do you assess ventilation status — Use bedside capnography or repeat clinical assessment; give high‑flow O2 and arrange transfer for definitive testing.

A malaria patient presents with metabolic acidosis, PaO2 80 mmHg, PaCO2 30 mmHg — what is the primary disturbance and how to manage — Primary metabolic acidosis; give IV fluids, correct electrolytes, monitor for respiratory compensation.

A TB patient on treatment develops a new pleural effusion; ABG shows PaO2 55 mmHg, PaCO2 38 mmHg — what does this indicate and what intervention is needed — Isolated hypoxemia (type I failure); insert chest tube if large, give O2, treat infection.
During surgery, the anesthetist notes a sudden drop in PaO2 to 45 mmHg — what immediate actions are required — Increase FiO2, check airway, consider pneumothorax or aspiration, obtain repeat ABG.

A patient with sickle cell disease presents with chest pain and dyspnoea; ABG shows PaO2 70 mmHg, PaCO2 48 mmHg, pH 7.32 — what complication is likely and how to treat — Acute chest syndrome with early hypercapnia; start antibiotics, O2, and consider exchange transfusion.

You have a patient with chronic liver disease and a normal PaO2 but low SaO2 — why might this occur and what does it mean — Hypoxaemia from shunting or anemia; ABG helps differentiate and guide transfusion or O2 therapy.
